title: How the web works, and your first page
goal: Understand what happens when you type an address, then build a complete HTML document from an empty file.

steps.title: Where everything lives
steps.body: Before any detail, hold this shape in your head. Every page you will ever write is this, with more inside it.
steps.tree: the whole document | +-- information ABOUT the page (not shown on screen) | +-- character set, viewport, description | +-- the text in the browser tab | +-- <body> everything the visitor actually SEES +-- <h1> the main heading +-- <p> a paragraph +-- ... and so on

steps.title: What actually happens when you open a site
steps.body:
Every time you open a web page, two machines have a very short conversation. Your laptop is the client. The machine storing the site is the server.

  1. You type an address. The browser asks a directory service which machine that name belongs to.
  2. The browser sends a request: "please send me this page".
  3. The server sends back a response - usually a block of HTML text.
  4. Your browser reads that text and paints it on screen.

The important part: the server sends text, not a picture. Everything you see is the browser's interpretation of that text. That is why two browsers can render the same page slightly differently, and why a missing bracket can wreck a layout.

steps.title: Tag vs element - the distinction that gets marks
steps.body:
A tag is the marker you type. An element is the whole thing: opening tag, content, closing tag.

<p>Hello</p>
  • <p> is the opening tag
  • Hello is the content
  • </p> is the closing tag
  • all three together are the paragraph element

A few elements have no content and therefore no closing tag - <br>, <hr>, <img>, <meta>. These are called empty or void elements.

steps.title: head is not the same as heading
steps.body:
This trips up more people in the first week than anything else, and it costs marks because the two words sound identical.

  • <head> - a section of the document holding information about the page. Nothing inside it is drawn on screen.
  • <h1> to <h6> - headings, which are visible text inside <body>.

If your heading is not appearing, check you have not put it inside <head> by mistake. The browser will simply not draw it, with no error message.

title: Metadata: the part of the page nobody sees
goal: Use the <head> section properly - character set, description, viewport - and know why each one matters.

steps.title: What lives in the head
steps.body: Four things matter in the head. Learn them in this order.
steps.tree:
<head>
 +-- <meta charset="UTF-8">              1. how to decode the bytes
 +-- <meta name="viewport" ...>          2. how to size it on a phone
 +-- <title>...</title>                  3. the tab, and the search result
 +-- <meta name="description" ...>       4. the grey text under the result

steps.title: Why bother with invisible tags
steps.body:
Nothing inside <head> is drawn on screen, so it feels optional. It is not. These few lines decide whether your page is readable on a phone, whether Google shows a sensible summary, and whether Hindi or a rupee symbol displays correctly.

ElementWhat it doesWhat breaks without it
<meta charset>Names the alphabet Accented and non-English characters become garbage
<title>Tab text, search headline Tab shows the file path; search results look broken
<meta name="viewport">Phone scaling Phones render a desktop page zoomed out and tiny
<meta name="description">Search summary Google invents its own summary from your text

  <title>Campus Book Exchange - buy and sell used textbooks</title>
  <meta name="description" content="A noticeboard for students to swap
        second-hand textbooks within the campus.">
  <meta name="author" content="Your Name">
</head>
lines: Always first. The browser must know the alphabet before it reads the rest of the file.
width=device-width means 'one CSS pixel = one phone pixel'. This single line is what makes a page mobile friendly.
Aim for 50-60 characters. Put the useful words first - search results cut off the end.

steps.title: charset must come first
steps.body:
The character set declaration has to appear within the first 1024 bytes of the document, and in practice that means first inside <head>.

The reason is circular and worth understanding: the browser cannot read the file until it knows how the bytes map to characters, so it makes an early guess. If it guesses wrong and only finds out later, it has to throw away what it read and start again - and in older browsers, it simply does not bother.

Symptom of getting this wrong: your rupee sign, your curly quotes or a student's name appear as â‚¹ or ÃƒÂ©. That is always a charset problem, never a font problem.

title: Headings, paragraphs, breaks and rules
goal: Use the six heading levels correctly and know the difference between a line break and a new paragraph.

steps.title: Heading levels are an outline, not sizes
steps.body: Think of headings as the contents page of a book. The level says where it sits in the outline, not how big it looks.
steps.tree:
<h1>  Sunrise Institute of Technology      the one page topic
 |
 +-- <h2>  Courses                          a major part of it
 |    +-- <h3>  CSE326 Internet Programming   something inside Courses
 |    +-- <h3>  CSE201 Data Structures
 |
 +-- <h2>  Admissions
      +-- <h3>  Eligibility

steps.title: Headings carry meaning, not size
steps.body:
HTML gives you <h1> down to <h6>. Beginners pick one by how big it looks. That is the wrong reason. Headings describe structure - the browser, search engines and screen readers all build a table of contents from them.

<h1>Internet Programming</h1>     <!-- the page's one subject -->
  <h2>Unit 1: HTML</h2>            <!-- a major section -->
    <h3>Lists</h3>                 <!-- a topic inside it -->
  <h2>Unit 2: CSS</h2>

Two rules that get marks: use exactly one <h1> per page, and never skip a level to get a smaller font. If h2 looks too big, that is a job for CSS, not for jumping to h4.

steps.title: <br> versus a new paragraph
steps.body:
Both push text onto the next line, so they look interchangeable. They are not.

  • <p> starts a new block of thought. The browser adds space above and below it.
  • <br> is a line break inside one thought - an address, a line of a poem, a verse.

Writing <br><br> to fake a gap between paragraphs is the classic beginner shortcut. It works visually and is wrong structurally: a screen reader announces one long run-on paragraph.

steps.title: Never skip a heading level
steps.body:
Going straight from <h1> to <h3> because h3 "looked the right size" is the single most common accessibility fault in student work, and it is explicitly examinable.

A screen-reader user can pull up a list of headings and jump around the page with it - it is their equivalent of skim-reading. A skipped level makes that outline nonsense, as if a book jumped from chapter 1 to section 1.1.3.

If a heading is the wrong size, fix it in CSS. Never pick a heading level for its appearance.

title: Text formatting, quotations and comments
goal: Choose formatting tags by meaning rather than by appearance, and quote sources properly.

steps.title: Meaning first, appearance second
steps.body: Several tags look the same on screen but mean different things. The examiner cares about the meaning.
steps.tree:
looks bold          means important       ->  <strong>
looks bold          just bold, no meaning ->  <b>
looks italic        means emphasis        ->  <em>
looks italic        just italic           ->  <i>
looks italic        the TITLE of a work   ->  <cite>
indented block      a quotation           ->  <blockquote cite="...">

steps.title: The pairs that look identical but are not
steps.body:
Four tags cause more confusion than the rest of Unit 1 combined, because two pairs render the same way.

TagLooks likeActually means
<strong>bold This matters. Screen readers stress it.
<b>bold Draw the eye, no extra importance - a keyword.
<em>italic Emphasis that changes the sentence's meaning.
<i>italic Different in kind - a species name, a foreign phrase.

Rule of thumb: if reading it aloud you would change your voice, use <strong> or <em>. If it just looks different on the page, use <b> or <i>. In an exam, "semantic" always means the first pair.

steps.title: The rest of the formatting family
steps.body:
• <mark> - highlighted, like a yellow marker pen
  • <small> - side comments, legal print, disclaimers
  • <del> and <ins> - removed and added text, as in a tracked edit
  • <sub> and <sup> - below and above the line: H2O, x2
  • <code> - a snippet of program text
  • <pre> - keeps your spaces and line breaks exactly as typed, which no other element does

Quoting other people

  • <q> - a short quote inside a sentence. The browser adds the quotation marks, so do not type them yourself.
  • <blockquote> - a long quote, indented as its own block.
  • cite attribute - the URL the quote came from.
  • <cite> element - the title of a work, not a person's name. This is the one people get wrong.

Comments

Comments are invisible on the page but fully visible in View Source. Never put a password or anything private in one.

steps.title: strong and b are not interchangeable
steps.body:
They render identically. They are still not the same, and this is a favourite short-answer question.

  • <strong> means this matters. A screen reader may change tone. Search engines weigh it.
  • <b> means draw this bold and nothing more - a keyword, a product name, stylistic only.

The same split applies to <em> (stress emphasis, changes the sentence's meaning) versus <i> (a technical term, a foreign phrase, a thought).

Rule of thumb: if reading it aloud you would lean on the word, use em or strong. If you would read it flat and it just looks different, use i or b.

title: Block vs inline, and semantic structure
goal: Predict how any element will flow on the page, and lay out a document with semantic sectioning elements.

steps.title: The shape almost every site shares
steps.body: This is the skeleton behind nearly every page on the web. Learn it once and page layout stops being guesswork.
steps.tree:
<body>
 +-- <header>        the masthead: site name, and usually the nav
 |    +-- <nav>          the MAIN navigation links
 |
 +-- <main>          the unique content of THIS page - exactly one
 |    +-- <section>      a themed group, which has a heading
 |    |    +-- <article>   one self-contained item
 |    |    +-- <article>
 |    +-- <aside>        related, but not essential
 |
 +-- <footer>        closing information

steps.title: Two ways an element occupies space
steps.body:
Every element behaves in one of two default ways.

Block-levelInline
WidthTakes the full lineOnly as wide as content
New line?Always starts oneFlows in the text
Height / marginRespects bothIgnores vertical ones
Can containBlock and inlineUsually inline only
Examplesdiv, p, h1-h6, ul, ol, li, section, article span, a, img, strong, em, code, br

The rule that catches everyone: a block element must not be placed inside an inline one. <a><div>...</div></a> was invalid for years. HTML5 now permits it around links specifically, but <span><p>...</p></span> is still wrong.

steps.title: Stop using div for everything
steps.body:
<div> is a block with no meaning at all. HTML5 added elements that look identical but say what the section IS:

  • <header> - introductory content of a page or section
  • <nav> - the main navigation links
  • <main> - the primary content. Only one per page.
  • <section> - a thematic grouping, normally with a heading
  • <article> - a self-contained piece that would still make sense if you copied it elsewhere
  • <aside> - related but tangential: a sidebar
  • <footer> - closing information

They render exactly like a div. The gain is that a screen reader can jump straight to <main>, and a search engine can tell your article from your sidebar.

steps.title: section or article? one question decides it
steps.body:
This is the classic exam question, and there is a single test that gets it right nearly every time:

Would this block still make sense if you copied it onto a completely different website?

  • Yes - a news item, a blog post, a product card, a comment. It is an <article>.
  • No, it only makes sense here - "Our Courses", "Contact us". It is a <section>.

Two more rules that carry marks: a <section> should always have a heading (if it has none, you wanted a <div>), and there is exactly one <main> per page.

Useful attributes on <ol>: type (1, A, a, I, i), start to begin at a number other than 1, and reversed to count down.

The one structural rule: <ul> and <ol> may contain only <li> as direct children. Loose text sitting straight inside a <ul> is invalid.

Nesting is where marks are lost. The only legal child of <ul> or <ol> is <li> - so a nested list must sit inside the <li> it belongs to, before that li closes.

Notice where </li> moved. That single line is the whole difference, and it is the thing to check first when a nested list renders strangely.

steps.title: Four kinds of link
steps.body:
<a href="https://example.com">External site</a>
<a href="about.html">Another page in my folder</a>
<a href="#contact">Jump to a section of this page</a>
<a href="mailto:me@example.com">Send an email</a>

Absolute paths start with https:// and point anywhere on the internet. Relative paths are worked out from the current file's folder - about.html means "next to me", ../index.html means "one folder up".

A fragment link (#contact) scrolls to whichever element has id="contact". The id must exist or nothing happens.

The target attribute

target="_blank" opens a new tab. When you use it on an external link, add rel="noopener" - without it the new page gets a JavaScript handle back to yours, which is a known security weakness.

steps.title: alt text is not optional
steps.body:
<img src="library.jpg" alt="Students reading in the campus library"
     width="600" height="400">
  • src - where the file is. No src, no image.
  • alt - what the picture shows. Read aloud to blind users, and displayed when the file fails to load.
  • width / height - reserve the space so the page does not jump around while the image downloads.

Write alt as a description, not a label. "Students reading in the campus library" is useful. "image1.jpg" or "photo" is noise. If a picture is purely decorative, use alt="" - empty, but present - so screen readers skip it silently.

To make an image clickable, put it inside the link: <a href="..."><img ...></a>.

steps.title: target="_blank" without rel="noopener" is a security bug
steps.body:
Opening a link in a new tab hands the new page a JavaScript reference back to yours, through window.opener. The page you linked to can then quietly redirect your tab to a fake login screen while the user is reading the new tab. It is called tabnabbing.

<a href="https://example.com"
   target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Read more</a>

  • noreferrer also stops sending which page they came from.

Modern browsers now imply noopener for target="_blank", but write it anyway: it is what the examiner expects, and it protects users on older browsers.

title: SVG graphics
goal: Draw shapes directly in HTML and understand why they never blur.

steps.title: How an SVG is put together
steps.body: SVG describes shapes with numbers instead of pixels, so it stays sharp at any size.
steps.tree:
<svg viewBox="0 0 200 120">      the coordinate system
 |                               "0,0 to 200,120", whatever the
 |                               displayed size turns out to be
 +-- <rect x y width height>       a rectangle
 +-- <circle cx cy r>              a circle
 +-- <line x1 y1 x2 y2>            a straight line
 +-- <text x y>...</text>          words
 +-- <polygon points="...">        a closed shape

steps.title: Pixels versus instructions
steps.body:
A JPG or PNG stores a grid of coloured dots. Enlarge it and the dots enlarge too, so it goes blurry. An SVG stores instructions - "draw a circle here, radius 40". The browser re-draws at whatever size is needed, so it is sharp on any screen.

SVG suits logos, icons, charts and diagrams. Photographs stay as JPG.

You can write SVG straight into your HTML - no separate file, no extra download - and style or script it like any other element.

steps.title: The basic shapes and the viewBox
steps.body:
<rect x="10" y="10" width="80" height="50" fill="teal">
<circle cx="60" cy="60" r="40" fill="orange">
<ellipse cx="60" cy="60" rx="50" ry="30">
<line x1="0" y1="0" x2="100" y2="100" stroke="black">
<polygon points="50,5 90,90 10,90" fill="purple">
<text x="20" y="50">Hello</text>

Coordinates start at the top-left corner. x grows to the right and y grows downwards - the opposite of a maths graph, which is the usual source of "why is my shape upside down".

viewBox

<svg width="300" height="200" viewBox="0 0 100 100">

viewBox="0 0 100 100" means "treat the drawing area as 100 by 100 units". The width and height then say how big to render it on the page. Because the two are separate, one drawing scales to any size without editing a single coordinate.

  <polygon points="50,25 75,70 25,70" fill="#7c3aed"></polygon>
  <text x="50" y="90" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle"
        fill="#ffffff">CSE326</text>

Rendered at 200px. Change these two numbers and nothing else needs editing.

SVG has no alt attribute, so this is how you describe it to a screen reader.

steps.title: viewBox is what makes it scale
steps.body:
width and height say how big the picture is on screen. viewBox says what coordinate system you are drawing in. Separating those two is the whole point of SVG.

<svg width="400" height="240" viewBox="0 0 200 120">

You draw in a 200×120 world; the browser paints it at 400×240, scaling everything perfectly. Change the width to 50 and the same code still draws cleanly.

Omit viewBox and the drawing is stuck at one fixed size - it will crop or leave blank space instead of scaling. If your SVG "does not resize", this is why.

steps.title: One pattern for all embedded media
steps.body: Video and audio share the same shape: a wrapper, several formats to choose from, then a fallback for anyone who can play none of them.
steps.tree:
<video controls poster="thumb.jpg">
 +-- <source src="clip.mp4"  type="video/mp4">     browser tries this first
 +-- <source src="clip.webm" type="video/webm">    then this
 +-- "Your browser cannot play this."              shown if all fail

<audio controls>                same idea, no picture
 +-- <source ...>

<iframe src="..." title="...">  someone else's page inside yours

steps.title: Native media elements
steps.body:
<audio src="song.mp3" controls></audio>

<video width="480" controls poster="cover.jpg">
  <source src="clip.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <source src="clip.webm" type="video/webm">
  Your browser cannot play this video.
</video>

Giving several <source> elements lets the browser pick the first format it supports. The text after them shows only if none work.

AttributeEffect
controlsShows play, pause, volume. Without it there is no way to start playback.
autoplayStarts on load - browsers block this unless the video is also muted.
mutedStarts silent. Required for autoplay.
loopRepeats forever.
posterStill image shown before play.
preloadnone / metadata / auto - how much to fetch up front.

These are boolean attributes: writing controls switches them on. There is no controls="false" - writing that still switches it ON, because the browser only checks whether the attribute is present.

steps.title: iframe - a page inside a page
steps.body:
<iframe src="https://example.com/map" width="600" height="400"
        title="Campus location map" loading="lazy"
        allowfullscreen></iframe>

An iframe embeds a whole separate document - a map, a video player, a form. Key attributes: title (required for accessibility - it is what a screen reader announces), loading="lazy" (do not download until scrolled near), and sandbox (restricts what the embedded page may do).

Not every site allows embedding. Many send a header that forbids it, and the frame stays blank - that is the remote site's choice, not your bug.

title: SEO: being found
goal: Write the markup that decides how a page appears in search results.

steps.title: What a search engine reads, in order
steps.body: A crawler never sees your design. It reads text, in roughly this order of importance.
steps.tree: 1. the clickable blue headline 2. <meta description> the grey summary underneath 3. <h1> what this page is about 4. <h2> <h3> how it is organised 5. link text "Admissions form", not "click here" 6. <img alt> what the pictures show 7. body text everything else

steps.title: What a search engine actually reads
steps.body:
A search engine cannot see your page. It reads the HTML and looks for signals about what the page is about. Most of those signals are things you already know how to write.

SignalWhere it shows up
<title>The blue clickable headline
<meta name="description"> The grey summary underneath
<h1> and heading order Tells the crawler the page's topic and outline
alt textLets images appear in image search
Link textDescribes the destination page
Semantic elementsSeparates real content from sidebars

Notice there is no special "SEO tag". Good SEO is mostly correct, honest HTML - the same choices that make a page accessible.

steps.title: Link text and the robots file
steps.body:
Compare these two:

Download the syllabus <a href="syl.pdf">here</a>.        <!-- weak -->
<a href="syl.pdf">Download the CSE326 syllabus (PDF)</a>   <!-- strong -->

The link text is the description of the destination. "Click here" describes nothing - and a screen-reader user listing the links on a page hears "here, here, here".

Two supporting files sit at the site root, not in your HTML:

  • robots.txt - asks crawlers which paths to skip
  • sitemap.xml - lists your pages so none are missed

You can also block one page with <meta name="robots" content="noindex">.

title: Best practices and validation
goal: Write markup that another person - and the W3C validator - can read without complaint.

steps.title: What the validator checks
steps.body: Before you submit anything, run it through validator.w3.org. It catches in seconds what can cost you marks.
steps.tree:
structure   ->  is every element closed, and closed in order?
nesting     ->  is a block element hiding inside an inline one?
attributes  ->  is every value in quotes? any duplicate ids?
required    ->  doctype, lang, charset, title, alt on every img
obsolete    ->  <center> <font> <big> - removed from HTML5

steps.title: The habits that separate a pass from a good grade
steps.body:
1. Close every element, in the right order. Last opened, first closed.
  2. Lowercase your tags and attributes. HTML tolerates <DIV>; every style guide forbids it.
  3. Quote every attribute value. class=my box silently becomes two attributes.
  4. Indent consistently - two spaces per level. This is how you spot a missing closing tag by eye.
  5. Choose elements by meaning, then style with CSS.
  6. Keep CSS and JavaScript in their own files rather than inline.
  7. Give every image an alt and every iframe a title.
  8. Comment the why, not the what. <!-- nav --> on a <nav> adds nothing.

Validation

The W3C validator at validator.w3.org reads your file and lists every structural error. It catches unclosed tags, duplicate ids and misnesting - exactly the bugs that produce a page that "looks fine on my laptop" and collapses elsewhere.

A duplicate id is the classic silent bug. Ids must be unique on a page; when two match, fragment links and scripts pick the first and appear to ignore the rest.

Elements nest like brackets in mathematics. The last one opened is the first one closed.

<!-- WRONG - they cross over -->
<p><strong>Important</p></strong>

<p><strong>Important</strong></p>

Browsers silently repair the first version, which is exactly what makes it dangerous: it looks fine on your machine and fails the validator. Two browsers may also repair it differently.

Indent your code one level per nesting level. Almost every mismatched tag becomes visible the moment the indentation is right.

Nearly every site you use has the same underlying skeleton. Once you can see it, laying out a page stops being guesswork.

<body>

    <nav>       <!-- the main links               -->
  <main>        <!-- the unique content, ONE only -->
    <section>   <!-- a themed group, has a heading-->

section vs article is the classic exam question. Ask yourself: would this block still make sense if you copied it onto a different website? If yes it is an <article>. If it only makes sense as part of this page, it is a <section>.

A blog post, a product card and a news item are articles. "Latest posts", "Our products" and "Contact us" are sections.

title: Tables, and merging cells with colspan and rowspan
goal: Build a properly structured data table and merge cells across columns and rows.

steps.title: The parts of a table
steps.body: A table has three row groups. Browsers and screen readers rely on them, and printers repeat the head on every page.
steps.tree:
<table>
 +-- <caption>        the table's title - FIRST child, always
 +-- <thead>          the heading row(s)
 |    +-- <tr>
 |         +-- <th scope="col">
 +-- <tbody>          the data rows
 |    +-- <tr>
 |         +-- <th scope="row">     a heading for THIS row
 |         +-- <td>                 a data cell
 +-- <tfoot>          totals or notes

steps.title: The parts of a table
steps.body:
Tables are for data - a timetable, a mark sheet, a price list. They are not for page layout; CSS does that job.

ElementWhat it is
<table>The table itself
<caption> Its title. Must be the first child of table
<thead>The header row group
<tbody>The data rows
<tfoot>Totals and summary rows
<tr>One row
<th>A header cell - bold and centred
<td>A data cell

Cells always live inside a <tr>. A <td> placed directly inside <table> is invalid, and browsers will quietly move it somewhere you did not intend.

steps.title: Merging cells
steps.body:
Two attributes do the merging, and mixing them up is a reliable way to lose marks.

  • colspan="2" - this cell stretches across 2 columns (sideways)
  • rowspan="3" - this cell stretches down 3 rows (downwards)

The rule that trips everyone: when a cell spans, the rows or columns it swallows must lose a cell. If a row normally has 4 cells and one of them has colspan="2", that row now needs only 3 cell tags - because the spanning cell is doing the work of two.

<tr>
  <td colspan="2">Monday and Tuesday</td>  <!-- covers 2 columns -->
  <td>Wednesday</td>                       <!-- so only 2 <td> here -->
</tr>

Count your cells row by row. If a table looks lopsided, you have almost certainly left an extra cell in a row that contains a span.

steps.title: colspan spreads sideways, rowspan reaches downwards
steps.body:
Everyone mixes these up once. Fix it with the direction of the word:

  • colspan="3" - this cell covers three columns, so it grows to the right.
  • rowspan="2" - this cell covers two rows, so it grows down.

The rule that catches people: when a cell spans down into the next row, that next row must have one fewer cell written, because the space is already taken.

<tr><th rowspan="2">Group A</th><td>18</td></tr>
<tr><td>16</td></tr>   <!-- no th here: the rowspan filled it -->

If your table develops a staircase of empty cells, you have written a cell that the span already accounted for.

title: Forms: labels, controls and grouping
goal: Build an accessible form using label, input, textarea, select, button, fieldset and legend.

steps.title: How a form is assembled
steps.body: Every control follows the same three-part pattern: a label, an input, and the id that ties them together.
steps.tree:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
 +-- <fieldset>                  a group of related controls
      +-- <legend>                  the group's title
      |
      +-- <label for="em">          -----+
      +-- <input id="em" name="email">   |  for="em" MUST equal id="em"
      |                             -----+
      +-- <select> + <option>
      +-- <textarea>
 +-- <button type="submit">

steps.title: Why every field needs a label
steps.body:
A <label> is not decoration. Tied to a field, it makes the text clickable (a much bigger tap target on a phone) and it is what a screen reader announces when the user reaches that field.

<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

The for attribute must match the input's id exactly. That pairing is the whole mechanism.

placeholder is not a label. Grey hint text vanishes the moment the user types, so they lose the only clue about what the field wanted. Examiners ask this. Use both: a label for the name, a placeholder for an example.

id versus name

  • id - links the label to the field, and must be unique on the page
  • name - the key the value is submitted under. No name, and the field is not sent at all

steps.title: The controls, and grouping them
steps.body:
• <input> - one-line field; the type decides what kind. Empty element, no closing tag.
  • <textarea> - multi-line. Always needs a closing tag, and its value goes between the tags, not in a value attribute.
  • <select> with <option> - a drop-down. Add selected to pre-choose one.
  • <button> - use type="submit" to send, type="button" for anything else.
  • <fieldset> with <legend> - draws a box round related fields and names the group. Essential for radio buttons, so the user hears "Gender: male" rather than just "male".
  • <progress> - shows how far something has got.

Useful attributes

required blocks submission while empty, readonly shows a value that cannot be edited but IS submitted, and disabled greys the field out and does not submit it. That last difference is a favourite exam question.

steps.title: id connects the label; name carries the data
steps.body:
Two attributes that look interchangeable and are not. Every input needs both, and they do completely different jobs.

  • id is for the browser. It is what <label for="..."> points at. Get it wrong and clicking the label does nothing.
  • name is for the server. It becomes the key when the form is submitted: email=asha@example.com. No name means the field is not sent at all - the commonest reason a form "loses" a field.

Why the label matters beyond accessibility: it makes the whole label text a click target. On a phone, that is the difference between hitting a radio button and missing it.

goal: Pick the right input type for each kind of data and let the browser do the first round of validation.

steps.title: Choosing the input type
steps.body: The type is not decoration. It changes the on-screen keyboard, the validation and the picker the browser offers.
steps.tree:
text       plain words
email      validates the @, email keyboard on phones
tel        numeric keypad on phones
number     min, max, step; spinner arrows
date       a calendar picker
password   masks the characters
radio      pick ONE from a group  -> share the same name
checkbox   independent on/off     -> different names
file       a file picker
submit     sends the form

steps.title: One tag, thirteen behaviours
steps.body:
Every one of these is <input>. Only the type changes - and with it the keyboard a phone shows, the picker that opens, and the validation the browser performs for free.

typeUse it forYou get free
textAny short textnothing
passwordSecretscharacters hidden
emailAddressesshape check, @ keyboard
numberQuantitiesmin, max, step, spinner
dateCalendar datesdate picker
timeTimes of daytime picker
fileUploadsfile chooser
checkboxZero or more choicestick boxes
radioExactly one of a groupmutual exclusion
rangeApproximate valuesa slider
submitSending the formsubmit action
resetClearing the formreset action
buttonAnything elsenothing built in

Radio buttons only work in a group. Give every radio in the group the same name - that is what makes selecting one clear the others. Different names means every button is its own group, and they will all stay selected. This is the single most common form bug.

steps.title: Validation without a line of JavaScript
steps.body:
The browser will check these for you before the form is ever sent:

  • required - must not be empty
  • min / max - smallest and largest value (numbers, dates, ranges)
  • step - the allowed interval, e.g. step="0.5"
  • minlength / maxlength - fewest and most characters
  • the type itself - email demands an @, number refuses letters

This is called client-side validation. It gives instant feedback, but a determined user can bypass it, so a real server must check again. For this course, knowing which attribute does which job is what earns the mark.

steps.title: Radio buttons: the same name is what groups them
steps.body:
This is the single most-tested detail in the forms topic, so it gets its own step.

Radio buttons are not grouped by being near each other, or by sitting in the same fieldset. They are grouped only by sharing an identical name. Same name, and selecting one clears the others. Different names, and every button turns on independently - which is a checkbox pretending to be a radio.

<input type="radio" id="am" name="slot" value="morning">
<label for="am">Morning</label>

<input type="radio" id="pm" name="slot" value="afternoon">
<label for="pm">Afternoon</label>

name is the same (slot) - that makes them one group. id is different - each label needs its own target. value differs - that is what actually gets sent.

Checkboxes are the mirror image: they are independent, so each normally gets its own name.

title: Accessibility: building pages everyone can use
goal: Make a page usable with a screen reader and a keyboard alone, using language, heading order, alt text, labels and ARIA.

steps.title: The five things that carry most of the benefit
steps.body: Accessibility has a long specification, but in coursework and in practice these five account for the overwhelming majority of real failures.
steps.tree: 1. so it is read in the right accent 2. heading order h1 -> h2 -> h3, never skipping 3. alt on every or alt="" if purely decorative 4.

steps.title: Who this is actually for
steps.body:
Accessibility is not a niche extra. Roughly one person in six has a disability that affects how they use a computer, and the same techniques help far more people than that: someone on a cracked phone screen in bright sunlight, someone with a broken mouse, someone on a slow connection where images never load.

There is a practical angle too. The structure that makes a page accessible is the same structure search engines read, which is why Unit 1's SEO lesson and this one keep arriving at the same advice.

The good news: almost all of it is writing correct HTML in the first place. Accessibility is mostly not an addition - it is the absence of mistakes.

steps.title: How a screen reader moves through a page
steps.body:
To understand the rules, picture how a blind user actually reads. They do not hear the page top to bottom - that would be unbearable. They jump.

  • Pull up a list of headings and jump to the interesting one. This is why heading order matters.
  • Jump between landmarks - header, nav, main, footer - to skip straight past the navigation.
  • Pull up a list of links, hearing only the link text. This is why five links all reading "click here" are useless.
  • Tab through the form controls, hearing each one's label.

Every rule below exists to make one of those four things work.

lines: A div has no meaning. It never appears in the headings list, so the page has no outline to navigate by.
A span cannot be reached by Tab and does nothing when you press Enter. A real link works with keyboard, middle-click, and 'open in new tab' for free.
A screen reader falls back to reading the file name aloud - 'lab dot jpg' - which tells the user nothing.
The user hears 'edit text, blank'. There is no way to know what to type.
A real button is focusable, announces itself as a button, and fires on both Enter and Space. Recreating that on a div takes four extra attributes and a keydown handler.

steps.title: alt text: what to write, and when to write nothing
steps.body:
The question to ask is not "what is in this picture?" but "if I removed the image, what would I need to say instead?"

  • Informative - describe the content. alt="Students working at machines in the Block 34 laboratory"
  • A link or a button - describe the destination or action, not the picture. alt="Download the prospectus"
  • Decorative - a divider, a background flourish. Use alt="", empty and deliberate. The screen reader then skips it silently.
  • Text inside the image - the alt must repeat that text.

There is a real difference between alt="" and no alt at all. Empty alt means "skip this, it carries no information". A missing alt makes the reader announce the file name. Never leave it off.

Do not begin with "Image of" or "Picture of" - the screen reader already says "image". And keep it to roughly one sentence.

steps.title: The first rule of ARIA is: do not use ARIA
steps.body:
That is the actual wording of the first rule in the W3C's authoring guide, and it sounds like a joke until you see why.

Native HTML elements come with behaviour built in. <button> is already focusable, already announces itself as a button, already fires on Enter and Space. Writing <div role="button" tabindex="0" aria-pressed="false"> plus a keydown handler recreates - badly - what one tag gave you free.

So use ARIA only when HTML genuinely has no element for the job, or to label something that would otherwise be ambiguous:

<!-- two navs on one page: which is which? -->
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">...</nav>
<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">...</nav>

<!-- an icon-only button has no visible text to read -->
<button aria-label="Close dialog">×</button>

Worth knowing for the exam: bad ARIA is worse than no ARIA. A wrong role overrides what the element really is, so the screen reader confidently announces something false.

steps.title: Three ways to attach CSS
steps.body:
CSS answers one question: what should this look like? HTML already said what things are.

WayLooks likeUse it
Inline<p style="color:red"> Almost never
Internal<style> in the head One-page demos
External<link rel="stylesheet"> Always, for real work

External wins because one file styles a hundred pages, and the browser caches it. Inline styles cannot be reused, cannot be overridden easily, and turn your HTML back into 1998.

The anatomy of a rule

selector {
  property: value;   /* this pair is a DECLARATION */
}

h1 {
  color: navy;
  font-size: 32px;

steps.title: The three selectors you use daily
steps.body:
• Element - p { } targets every paragraph
  • Class - .card { } targets class="card". Reusable, use it constantly.
  • Id - #header { } targets id="header". Unique, use it rarely.

Combining them

h1, h2      { }   /* group: both h1 AND h2        */
article p   { }   /* descendant: any p inside an article */
article > p { }   /* child: only DIRECT children  */
.card.wide  { }   /* element with BOTH classes    */

The space in article p means "somewhere inside". The > means "directly inside, one level down". That single space is a real operator, and forgetting it changes what you select.

title: The cascade and specificity
goal: Predict which rule wins when two rules target the same element.

steps.title: How the winner is chosen
steps.body: When two rules set the same property, the browser works down this list and stops at the first thing that separates them.
steps.tree:
1. !important            avoid - it ends the argument badly
2. inline style="..."    1000
3. #id                    100
4. .class  [attr]  :hover  10
5. element  ::before        1
6. if still tied -> whichever is written LAST wins

steps.title: Why is my CSS being ignored?
steps.body:
This is the question that dominates every CSS beginner's life. The style is written correctly and nothing happens. The answer is almost always specificity: another rule is more specific, so it wins.

When two rules set the same property on the same element, the browser decides in this order:

  1. Importance - !important beats everything
  2. Specificity - the more specific selector wins
  3. Order - if still tied, the one written LAST wins

Counting specificity

Score each selector as three numbers - (ids, classes, elements):

SelectorScoreBeats
p0,0,1nothing much
.intro0,1,0any element selector
article p0,0,2p
.card p0,1,1article p
#intro1,0,0any number of classes

Compare left to right, like version numbers. One id beats any number of classes. One class beats any number of elements. That is why #intro (1,0,0) defeats body article div p.text (0,1,4).

steps.title: Four rules, one paragraph
steps.code:

Red - the id beats the class.
lines: Two elements beat one, so blue wins.
A single class outranks any number of element selectors.
A single id outranks any number of classes.
If your rule is ignored, count the specificity of whatever is beating it - do not reach for !important.

steps.title: Inheritance, and !important
steps.body:
Some properties pass down to children automatically - color, font-family, line-height. Set them once on body and the whole page follows.

Others do not inherit at all - border, padding, margin, background. That is sensible: you rarely want every child to repeat the parent's border.

!important

p { color: red !important; }

It wins regardless of specificity. Treat it as a last resort. Once one !important exists, overriding it needs another, and within a month the stylesheet is unmaintainable. The professional habit is to fix the specificity instead.

steps.title: Specificity is compared column by column, not added up
steps.body:
Write the score as three columns: (ids, classes, elements).

#hero            -> (1, 0, 0)
.card .title     -> (0, 2, 0)
article section p-> (0, 0, 3)

The browser compares the first column first. Only if those tie does it look at the second. So #hero at (1,0,0) beats .card .title at (0,2,0) - not because 100 > 20, but because any id beats any number of classes.

This is why one hundred classes still lose to a single id. It is not arithmetic; it is a tie-break sequence.

title: The box model, colours and units
goal: Control size and spacing predictably, and stop fighting unexpected widths.

steps.title: The box around every element
steps.body: Every element on a page is a rectangle made of four layers, from the inside out.

steps.title: Every element is a box
steps.body:
From the middle outwards:

  1. content - the text or image itself
  2. padding - space INSIDE the border. Takes the background colour.
  3. border - the line around it
  4. margin - space OUTSIDE the border. Always transparent.

The distinction that gets examined: padding is inside and is coloured by the background; margin is outside and is always see-through. If you want space that shows the element's colour, that is padding.

Shorthand order is clockwise from the top

padding: 10px;                /* all four sides        */
padding: 10px 20px;           /* top+bottom | left+right */
padding: 10px 20px 15px;      /* top | left+right | bottom */
padding: 10px 20px 15px 5px;  /* top | right | bottom | left */

Remember it as a clock face: 12, 3, 6, 9.

steps.title: box-sizing - the one line that fixes everything
steps.body:
By default, width sets the width of the CONTENT only. Add padding and border and the element gets bigger than the number you wrote.

.box {
  width: 200px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 5px solid;
}
/* actual width on screen = 200 + 20 + 20 + 5 + 5 = 250px */

This surprises everyone. The fix is one rule at the top of every real stylesheet:

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}
/* now width:200px MEANS 200px, padding and border included */

Units worth knowing

UnitMeansUse for
pxfixed pixelsborders, small gaps
%of the parentwidths
emof the PARENT's font sizespacing near text
remof the ROOT font sizefont sizes - predictable
vw/vh1% of viewportfull-screen sections

Prefer rem for text: it respects the reader's browser font setting, which px ignores. That is an accessibility win.

steps.title: Five values, one question each

Every element starts at position: static - it sits where the normal flow puts it, and top/left do nothing.

ValueMoves relative toLeaves a gap?

An absolute element measures its offsets from the nearest ancestor that is itself positioned - meaning anything except static. If no ancestor qualifies, it keeps climbing and lands on the page itself.

steps.title: Container properties versus item properties
steps.body: Half of Flexbox confusion is applying a property to the wrong element. These go on the container; those go on the children.
steps.tree:
.row { display: flex; }        <-- ON THE CONTAINER
   +-- justify-content     spacing along the main axis
   +-- align-items         alignment across the other axis
   +-- flex-direction      row (default) or column
   +-- flex-wrap           allow a second line
   +-- gap                 space between items

.card { ... }                  <-- ON EACH CHILD
   +-- flex: grow shrink basis
   +-- align-self           override align-items for one item
   +-- order                move it without touching the HTML

steps.title: One dimension, two axes
steps.body:
Flexbox lays children out along ONE line - a row or a column. You set display: flex on the parent, and the children become flex items automatically.

.nav {
  display: flex;                    /* children now sit in a row */
  gap: 16px;                        /* space BETWEEN them        */
  justify-content: space-between;   /* along the MAIN axis        */
  align-items: center;              /* along the CROSS axis       */
}

With flex-direction: row (the default), the main axis runs left-to-right and the cross axis runs top-to-bottom. Switch to column and the two swap over - which is why justify-content suddenly controls vertical position. That swap is the single most confusing thing about Flexbox, and knowing it removes most of the confusion.

goal: Lay out a full page in two dimensions and make it adapt to any screen.

steps.title: Grid is two-dimensional; Flexbox is one
steps.body: Choose by the shape of the problem, not by which you learned first.
steps.tree:
Flexbox   ONE direction: a row OR a column
          nav bars, button groups, a row of cards
          items decide their own size

Grid      TWO directions at once: rows AND columns
          page layouts, galleries, anything aligned
          the container defines the tracks

repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr))
   |         |            |      |
   |         |            |      +-- may grow to fill the space
   |         |            +-- but never narrower than 180px
   |         +-- fit as many columns as will fit
   +-- repeat the pattern

steps.title: Grid does two dimensions
steps.body:
Flexbox handles a line. Grid handles rows and columns at once - a whole page layout, a photo gallery, a dashboard.

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr;   /* sidebar, then the rest */
  gap: 20px;
}

fr means "one share of the space left over". Two columns of 1fr 1fr split it evenly; 2fr 1fr gives the first twice as much.

The one line worth memorising

grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr));

Read it as: "fit as many columns as you can, each at least 220px, each sharing the leftover space." That single line gives a responsive gallery with no media query at all - it adds and removes columns by itself as the window changes.

steps.title: Media queries and mobile-first
steps.body:
A media query applies rules only at certain sizes.

/* base rules: written for the SMALLEST screen */
.layout { display: block; }

/* then add complexity as space allows */
@media (min-width: 700px) {
  .layout { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr; }
}

Mobile-first means writing the phone layout as the default and using min-width queries to add layout for bigger screens. It produces simpler CSS than the reverse, and phones - which are most of your users - do the least work.

None of this functions without the viewport meta tag from Unit 1:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

Forget that line and every media query is ignored, because the phone pretends to be a 980px desktop.

The classic responsive gallery needs no breakpoints at all:

title: Pseudo-classes, variables, transitions and animations
goal: Style interactive states, reuse values with variables, and add motion that improves rather than distracts.

steps.title: The four modern-CSS ideas in one place
steps.body: These four turn a static stylesheet into a designed interface.

steps.title: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements
steps.body:
A pseudo-class (one colon) styles an element in a particular STATE. A pseudo-element (two colons) styles a PART of it, or invents a new part.

/* pseudo-CLASSES - a state */
a:hover        { }   /* mouse is over it       */
input:focus    { }   /* keyboard is in it      */
li:first-child { }   /* first among siblings   */
li:nth-child(2n){ }  /* every second one       */
input:required { }   /* has the required attr  */

/* pseudo-ELEMENTS - a part */
p::first-line  { }
p::before      { content: "-> "; }
p::after       { content: " <-"; }

:focus is not optional. A keyboard user navigating with Tab has no idea where they are without a visible focus style. Removing outlines with outline: none and putting nothing back is a genuine accessibility failure - and your CA1 syllabus explicitly mentions focus styles.

Attribute selectors

input[type="email"]   { }   /* exactly     */
a[href^="https"]      { }   /* starts with */
a[href$=".pdf"]       { }   /* ends with   */
a[href*="lpu"]        { }   /* contains    */

steps.title: Variables, transitions, animations
steps.body:
Custom properties (CSS variables)

:root {
  --brand: #E07B1E;
  --gap: 16px;
}
.btn { background: var(--brand); padding: var(--gap); }

Declare them on :root so the whole document can see them. Change one line and the entire theme changes - which is exactly how this portal's saffron and green are defined.

Transitions - smooth a change you already have

.btn {
  background: var(--brand);
  transition: background .2s ease, transform .12s ease;
}
.btn:hover  { background: #b45309; }
.btn:active { transform: translateY(1px); }

Put transition on the NORMAL state, not on :hover - otherwise it animates going in and snaps coming out.

Animations - motion without a trigger

@keyframes fadeUp {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(12px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
}
.card { animation: fadeUp .4s ease both; }

steps.title: The transition goes on the base rule, not on :hover
steps.body:
This one catches nearly everybody. Put the transition inside :hover and it only exists while hovering - so the element eases in smoothly and then snaps back the instant the pointer leaves.

/* WRONG - smooth in, snaps out */
.btn:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); transition: transform .2s; }

/* RIGHT - smooth both ways */
.btn       { transition: transform .2s ease; }
.btn:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); }

The rule: the transition belongs wherever the property normally lives. Also style :focus-visible alongside :hover - keyboard users never hover, and removing the focus outline without replacing it makes a page unusable for them.
